## [0:05–0:08] Learning Objectives

*[Advance to Learning Objectives slide.]*

Here's what we're aiming for today. Notice that none of these say 
"memorize functions." The functions you can always look up. What 
I want you to walk away with is the *reading* — the ability to look 
at a pipeline and understand what it's doing and why.

The last bullet is the one I care about most: reading wrangling code 
as a narrative of analytical decisions. We'll come back to that 
phrase a few times today.

---

## [0:08–0:13] Data Is Never Ready

*[Advance to "Data is rarely in the format we need" slide.]*

Let me start with a confession. The book says data is "rarely, if 
ever, in the format we need." I would go further. In ten years of 
doing this work, I have never — not once — received a dataset that 
was exactly ready to analyze. Not once.

And this is not because data collectors are sloppy. It's because 
**the format that makes sense for collecting data is almost never 
the format that makes sense for analyzing it.**

Think about how you collect data in the field or the lab. You might 
have one row per observation, or one sheet per site, or one column 
per species. That's intuitive when you're *recording*. But when 
you're *modeling*, you need `species` to be a column, not a set of 
column names spread across your spreadsheet.

This mismatch is not a failure. It's just reality. And `dplyr` and 
`tidyr` are our tools for navigating that reality.

---

## [0:13–0:16] Enter dplyr and tidyr

*[Advance to "Enter dplyr and tidyr" slide.]*

Two packages. One job each.

`dplyr` handles transformations of rows and columns — keeping 
columns, filtering rows, creating new variables, summarizing groups. 
Think of it as the workhorse for changing what's *in* your data.

`tidyr` handles reshaping — changing the *structure* of your data 
frame. Wide to long, long to wide, splitting columns, combining them.

You'll use both in almost every real analysis. And once you know 
them, you'll wonder how you ever managed without them.

---

## [0:16–0:24] Motivating Example 1 — Pseudocode Warm-Up

*[Advance to "Motivating Example 1: Summarizing" slide.]*

Before I show you any code, I want to do something. I want you to 
think.

Here's the problem. We have a table of salmon lengths. Multiple fish 
measured across multiple years. And we want to know: what was the 
average length per year?

*[Point to the table on the slide.]*

Look at this data. Before you think about R at all — what are the 
steps? In plain English. What would you do if you were solving this 
by hand?

I'm going to give you 90 seconds. Drop your answer in the chat — 
just a few words, don't overthink it. What are the steps?

*[Start timer. Watch chat. After 90 seconds, read a few responses 
aloud.]*

*[Common correct responses: group by year / find all the 1990 rows / 
then calculate average / then do the same for each year.]*

Yes. Exactly. You said it in different ways but you all got to the 
same place:

1. Separate the data by year
2. Calculate the average length within each year
3. Collect the results

That's it. That's the analysis. Now watch how closely the code 
matches what you just said.

---

## [0:24–0:27] Motivating Example 1 — The Code

*[Advance to "Motivating Example 1: The Code" slide.]*

```r
length_data %>% 
  group_by(year) %>% 
  summarize(mean_length_cm = mean(length_cm))
```

Read it out loud with me — use "then" for each `%>%`:

*"Take the data, **then** group by year, **then** summarize by 
calculating mean length."*

That's three lines of code. Three lines that do exactly what you 
described in the chat. That's the power of `dplyr` — it lets you 
write your reasoning as code.

The `%>%` symbol is doing the work of connecting those steps. We'll 
spend real time on it in a few minutes. For now, just notice how 
readable this is.

---

## [0:27–0:33] Motivating Example 2 — The Wide Data Problem

*[Advance to "Motivating Example 2: Reshaping" slide.]*

Okay, second example. This one is a little sneakier.

Here's a table that looks completely reasonable. Sites in rows, years 
in columns. You've probably seen data like this. It's actually a very 
natural way to record it — you add a column for each new year, each 
row is a place. Clean, intuitive.

*[Point to the wide table on the slide.]*

Now here's the problem. I want to fit a model: length as a function 
of year. In R that would be `lm(length ~ year)`.

*[Pause.]*

Where is `year` in this table?

*[Wait a beat.]*

It's not a column. It's a set of column *names*. And `lm()` can't 
work with that — it needs `year` to be a column with actual values in 
it, one per row.

This is the moment where a lot of people get stuck. The data looks 
fine. But the *shape* of the data is incompatible with the analysis 
you want to do.

This is what `tidyr` fixes.

---

## [0:33–0:36] Motivating Example 2 — The Code

*[Advance to "Motivating Example 2: The Code" slide.]*

```r
site_data %>% 
  pivot_longer(-site, 
               names_to = "year", 
               values_to = "length")
```

One function — `pivot_longer()` — and the years that were column 
names become values in a column called `year`. Now `lm(length ~ year)` 
works.

We'll spend a lot of time on `pivot_longer()` in Lecture 2. For now, 
I just want you to see that reshaping is possible and that it's 
readable. The arguments tell you exactly what's happening: the column 
*names* go into a column called `year`, the column *values* go into 
a column called `length`.

---

## [0:36–0:40] Function Reference — Tour of the Toolbox

*[Advance to "Key Functions We'll Use" slide.]*

This is a reference slide. You're not memorizing this today — you're 
getting oriented.

On the left, `dplyr` functions. These are your verbs for 
transformation: select columns, filter rows, mutate (create or 
change) columns, rename, group, summarize, arrange.

On the right, `tidyr` functions. These are your verbs for 
reshaping: pivot longer, pivot wider, separate a column into parts, 
unite parts into one column.

Seven plus four. Eleven functions. That's genuinely most of what you 
need for the majority of data wrangling you will ever do in your 
scientific career.

*[Pause for effect.]*

You'll use all of these in the activity. You'll use most of them in 
your final project. Let's get to know them.

---

## [0:40–0:45] Dataset Introduction

*[Advance to "Our Dataset: Alaska Salmon Catches" slide.]*

We're going to work with a real dataset for this whole chapter. 
Commercial salmon catches from Alaska, 1878 to 1997. Five species — 
Chinook, Sockeye, Coho, Pink, and Chum — across 18 fishing regions.

This is real data from the KNB data repository, which is exactly the 
kind of publicly archived scientific data you'll encounter in your 
own work.

```r
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)

catch_original <- read_csv(
  "https://knb.ecoinformatics.org/knb/d1/mn/v2/object/df35b.302.1"
)
```

Notice we're loading three packages: `dplyr`, `tidyr`, and `readr`. 
You'll need all three. And in the activity, this will be your 
first step — get the data in, then start exploring it.

---

## [0:45–0:49] Package Masking

*[Advance to "A Note on Package Masking" slide.]*

When you load `dplyr`, you will see a warning message that looks a 
little alarming:

```
The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
    filter, lag
```

I want to take a moment on this because students often panic when 
they see it, and they shouldn't.

This message is R telling you that `dplyr` has a function called 
`filter()`, and `stats` — which R loads automatically — also has a 
function called `filter()`. Since you loaded `dplyr` after `stats`, 
R will use `dplyr`'s version by default.

This is almost always what you want. But if you ever need to be 
explicit — to tell R "no, I mean the *stats* version" — you write:

`stats::filter()`

That double-colon syntax is how you call a specific package's 
function by name. Useful to know, rarely needed in practice.

Does anyone have a question about this before we move on? 
Drop it in chat.

*[Pause briefly. Address any questions.]*

---

## [0:49–0:54] Data Exploration

*[Advance to "Step 1: Explore Before You Transform" slide.]*

Rule number one of data wrangling: **explore before you transform**.

This is the equivalent of reading a paper before you cite it. You 
need to know what you're working with before you start changing it.

Here are the five exploration functions I use at the start of every 
new dataset:

```r
colnames(catch_original)    # what are the columns?
head(catch_original)        # what do the first rows look like?
summary(catch_original)     # what are the ranges and types?
unique(catch_original$Region)  # what are the distinct values?
View(catch_original)        # look at the whole thing (in console)
```

I want to call out `View()` specifically. Use it in the console, not 
in a code chunk. If you put it in a code chunk and render your 
document, it will try to open a viewer window during rendering and 
cause problems. Console only.

---

## [0:54–0:57] Why Explore First

*[Advance to "Why Explore First?" slide.]*

I want to give you an analogy that I think makes this concrete.

Reading your data before wrangling it is like reading a paper's 
methods section before jumping to the results. You need the context. 
You need to understand how the data was collected, what the variables 
mean, what the units are, before you can interpret anything.

Specifically, exploration helps you catch four things:

First — was the data read in correctly? Sometimes column types get 
mangled on import. A number becomes a character. A date becomes a 
number. You want to know this *now*, not after you've run twenty 
lines of code on top of it.

Second — are there unexpected data types? We're about to see a 
beautiful real-world example of this with the Chinook column. Stay 
tuned.

Third — missing values. Where are they? How many? Does the pattern 
matter?

Fourth — structure. How many rows? How many columns? What are the 
unique values in the key columns?

Explore first. Always.

---

## [0:57–1:02] The Pipe Operator

*[Advance to "The Pipe Operator" slide.]*

Okay. The pipe. This is the thing that makes `dplyr` and `tidyr` so 
readable, and it's worth spending real time on.

The pipe `%>%` does one thing: it takes whatever is on its left and 
passes it as the first argument to the function on its right.

Let me show you the before and after.

**Without the pipe:**

```r
df_filtered <- filter(df, ...)
df_selected <- select(df_filtered, ...)
```

I have to name intermediate objects. `df_filtered` exists only so 
that I can pass it to `select()`. That's cognitive overhead — now I 
have to track a variable that doesn't mean anything except "the 
result of the previous step."

**With the pipe:**

```r
df_cleaned <- df %>% 
    filter(...) %>%
    select(...)
```

No intermediate objects. The output of `filter()` flows directly 
into `select()`. The pipeline reads top to bottom like a recipe.

---

## [1:02–1:06] Reading the Pipe

*[Advance to "Reading Code with the Pipe" slide.]*

Here's the mental model I want you to use.

The assignment operator `<-` reads as **"gets"**.  
The pipe `%>%` reads as **"then"**.

So this:

```r
df_cleaned <- df %>% 
    filter(...) %>%
    select(...)
```

Reads as: *"The cleaned data frame **gets** the original data, 
**then** a filter, **then** a select."*

That's a sentence. A complete thought. A description of what you 
did and in what order.

This is what I mean when I say wrangling code is a narrative of 
analytical decisions. Each step in the pipe is a decision you made. 
The pipe makes the sequence of those decisions visible and readable.

When you read someone else's wrangling code, you should be able to 
narrate it in plain English. When you write your own, you should be 
able to explain why each step is there.

---

## [1:06–1:09] Benefits and Tradeoffs of Pipes

*[Advance to "Benefits and Tradeoffs of Pipes" slide.]*

Let me be honest with you — pipes are not always the right choice.

The benefits are real: no intermediate objects, sequential readability, 
easy to add or remove steps.

But when you're debugging, a long pipe can be a nightmare. If 
something's wrong, you have to figure out which step is the culprit. 
And you can't easily inspect intermediate results without breaking 
the pipe apart.

The practical advice: chain steps that belong together. When you've 
completed a meaningful stage — say, you've cleaned the data — save 
it to an object before continuing. That object becomes a checkpoint. 
You can inspect it, verify it looks right, and continue from there.

We'll see this pattern in action with the salmon data.

---

## [1:11–1:15] Setting Up the Document

*[Advance to "Setting Up Your Analysis Document" slide.]*

Before the activity, the book asks you to do something smart: 
outline your Quarto document before you start writing code.

Here's the structure it suggests:

- Data Sources
  - Read in the data
  - Explore data
- Clean and Reshape Data
  - select, quality check, mutate, pivot...
  - rename, mutate, group_by, summarize...
  - filter, arrange, separate, unite

This is literate programming in action. You're writing the structure 
of your analysis — the narrative — before you write the code. The 
code fills in the blanks.

In the activity, start here. Create your Quarto doc, add these 
headings, then work through the sections one at a time with the 
textbook as your guide.

# Instructor Notes

## Common Questions to Anticipate

**"What's the difference between `%>%` and `|>`?"**  
The native pipe `|>` was introduced in R 4.1. They work almost 
identically for our purposes. The book uses `%>%` so we'll use that 
throughout. If students have seen `|>` elsewhere, that's fine — 
both are valid.

**"Do I need to load all three packages every time?"**  
Yes, every new R session. That's what the library chunk in your 
Quarto document is for. Run it first, every time.

**"Why does the data have to come from a URL?"**  
It doesn't — the URL just means everyone gets the same version of 
the data without needing to download a file. In your own projects, 
you'll read from local files in your `data/` folder.

## Timing Adjustments

If you're running long, the "Why Explore First" slide (0:54) can 
be shortened to 90 seconds — just name the four things without 
elaborating. The pipe benefits and tradeoffs slide can also be 
cut to 90 seconds.

If you're running short, the motivating examples are expandable — 
ask students to narrate the wide data problem in their own words 
before revealing the solution.

## Breakout Option

If you want to add interaction around the pipe section, you can 
send students to breakout rooms for 3 minutes with the question: 
"Write the pipeline with the pipe, and the equivalent code without 
the pipe. Which do you find more readable and why?" Quick debrief 
on return. This adds ~5 minutes so cut from the tradeoffs section.
